fields.Front: Define domain, relation schema and relation (relation state) formally.
fields.Back:
DOMAIN D: a set of ATOMIC values with a data type specified ('10-character string', 'positive integer'); plainly 'it really is just the data type', possibly limited - all USA phone numbers, employee ages 16-100, department IDs.
RELATION SCHEMA R(A1, ..., An): a relation name R plus a list of attributes, each Aj naming a ROLE played by some domain D.
RELATION / relation state r(R): a set of n-tuples {t1, ..., tm}, each tuple an ordered list <v1, ..., vn> with each vi in dom(Ai) or null.

fields.Front: BOOK(Title, ISBN, Author, YearPublished, Publisher) with four rows: give its degree, cardinality and two domains.
fields.Back: Degree 5 (five attributes/columns); cardinality 4 ('four books, four tuples, four rows'). Domains: YearPublished - integers, 'maybe from 1900 to 2000-and-whatever'; ISBN - a letter followed by three digits (e.g. A781), simplified from real ISBNs. Relation schema: Book(Title, ISBN, Author, YearPub, Pub); R is Book.

fields.Front: Define the Cartesian product and give D1 x D2 for D1 = {2,4}, D2 = {1,3,5}. What is a relation on it?
fields.Back: The Cartesian product is ALL POSSIBLE tuples that can be produced from every value of every domain. D1 x D2 = {(2,1), (2,3), (2,5), (4,1), (4,3), (4,5)} - 6 pairs = 2 x 3. A mathematical relation is ANY SUBSET of it, e.g. R = {(2,5), (4,1)} - 'this would be a table'.

fields.Front: APPLICATION: D1 = {Simpson, Flanders, Smithers}, D2 = {Homer, Ned}, D3 = {40, 30}. How many tuples in D1 x D2 x D3, how do you list them, and how many rows/attributes can a relation over them have?
fields.Back: 3 x 2 x 2 = 12 triples. List systematically: fix the first value, then the second, then run through the third - (Simpson, Homer, 40), (Simpson, Homer, 30), (Simpson, Ned, 40), (Simpson, Ned, 30), then Flanders, then Smithers. A relation is ANY subset: 3 rows, 5 rows, or even all 12 - but it always has exactly 3 attributes.

fields.Front: Why does the Cartesian product matter for relations, and can you always list a whole domain?
fields.Back: Because a relation over those attributes is a SUBSET of the Cartesian product: each element of the product is one possible tuple, and a table is some of those tuples. No, you cannot always list every value (e.g. the real numbers); the domain is simply the set of possible values an attribute can take.

fields.Front: Textbook (Elmasri §5.1.1): what three things define a domain, and what does it mean that an attribute is 'the name of a role played by a domain'?
fields.Back:
A domain is given a NAME, a DATA TYPE and a FORMAT - for example Usa_phone_numbers declared as a character string (ddd)ddd-dddd whose first three digits are a valid area code, or Employee_ages as an integer between 15 and 80. Extra interpretation may be attached, such as the unit of measurement for Person_weights. These are called LOGICAL DEFINITIONS of domains.
Each attribute Ai is the NAME OF A ROLE played by some domain D in relation schema R, with D = dom(Ai). That is why SEVERAL ATTRIBUTES MAY SHARE ONE DOMAIN: in the book's STUDENT relation, Home_phone and Office_phone are two roles of Usa_phone_numbers, and Mobile_phone could be a third. The attribute NAME is what distinguishes their meanings.

fields.Front: Textbook (Elmasri §5.1.3): what do R, r, t, R.A, t[Ai] and t[Au, Aw, Az] mean in the book's notation?
fields.Back:
Uppercase Q, R, S: relation NAMES (schemas). Lowercase q, r, s: relation STATES. t, u, v: tuples.
R.A: attribute A qualified by the relation it belongs to (STUDENT.Name), needed because the same name may be used in different relations; within one relation all attribute names must be distinct.
t[Ai], t.Ai (or t[i]): the value of attribute Ai in tuple t.
t[Au, Aw, ..., Az]: the SUBTUPLE of those values, e.g. t[Ssn, Gpa, Age].
Also: DEGREE is also called ARITY; the schema is the relation INTENSION and the state is the relation EXTENSION.

fields.Text: Formal to everyday: relation = {{c1::table}}, attribute = {{c1::column}}, tuple = {{c1::row}}, degree = number of columns/attributes, cardinality = number of rows/tuples.

Big {{c1::R}} is the NAME of the relation schema (Student, Prof, Patient) - the description; little {{c1::r}} is the actual data, the set of {{c1::tuples}} at a moment in time (the relation state). Another way to think of a tuple is as an instance of the relation, e.g. the student Homer Simpson.

In a tuple t = <v1, ..., vn> the values are ordered by {{c1::the order of the attributes in the schema}} (v1 belongs to A1), and any vi may be {{c1::null}}. Her example schema is Student({{c1::StudentNumber, WesternUserID, FirstName, LastName}}).

The {{c1::cardinality}} of a relation is its number of rows - different from last week's {{c1::cardinality ratio}} ({{c1::1:1, 1:N, M:N}}) on an ER relationship. Same word, two meanings; expect a question that tests whether you keep them apart.

A domain is a set of {{c1::atomic}} values with a {{c1::data type}} specified; a relation schema is written {{c1::R(A1, A2, ..., An)}}; a relation state r(R) is a set of n-tuples, each an ordered list of values from dom(Ai) or null.

Textbook (Elmasri §5.1.1): the total number of tuples that could ever exist in any state of R is {{c1::the product of the cardinalities of all its domains}}, |dom(A1)| x ... x |dom(An)|, and an actual relation state is {{c1::a subset}} of that Cartesian product reflecting the valid tuples at that moment.

Textbook (Elmasri §5.1.2): NOTATION - avoid the phrase {{c1::relation instance}}; the book uses relation or {{c1::relation state}} for the whole set of tuples and reserves the word instance for {{c1::a single tuple or row}}, matching Chapter 2's use of instance for a single record.
